front: What does a PCIe x16 slot typically host?
back: A discrete GPU / high-bandwidth video card.

front: Is PCIe serial or parallel?
back: Serial. That is why it is faster than older parallel buses like PCI/PATA.

front: M.2 vs NVMe — which is the form factor?
back: M.2 is the form factor. NVMe is the protocol. An M.2 drive can be NVMe or SATA.

front: Rank storage from fastest to slowest (this guide).
back: PCIe → M.2/NVMe → SATA 3 (600 MB/s) → SATA 2 → SATA 1 → PATA.

front: Single-layer Blu-ray capacity?
back: About 25 GB.

front: Single-layer DVD capacity?
back: About 4.7 GB.

front: PSU: wall vs PC current type
back: Wall = AC in. Components need DC out. The PSU converts AC → DC.

front: Standard PC PSU DC rails
back: +3.3V, +5V, +12V, and −12V (rare). Not +4.3V, +8V, or +110V DC.

front: What is a redundant power supply?
back: A backup PSU so the system keeps running if the primary fails — common on servers.

front: Hot-swappable means…
back: You can insert/remove the device without turning system power off (after proper OS handling).

front: RAID 5 minimum disks and method
back: 3 disks. Striping with parity. Survives one disk failure.

front: Best slot for a video card
back: PCIe x16. PCIe x128 is not a real standard. AGP is obsolete.

front: Windows 11 TPM requirement
back: TPM 2.0 is mandatory and often blocks upgrades.

front: Windows 11 RAM and storage minima (this guide)
back: 4 GB RAM (8 GB recommended) and 64 GB storage.

front: Windows Home vs Pro (domain / BitLocker / RDP)
back: Home cannot join a domain, no BitLocker, no RDP host. Pro can.

front: 32-bit to 64-bit Windows
back: Clean install only. No in-place upgrade.

front: Boot sequence in order
back: POST → boot loader → kernel load → logon → shell/desktop.

front: When do you pick NTFS vs exFAT vs FAT32?
back: NTFS internal/Windows security. exFAT USB/cross-platform. FAT32 legacy only (4 GB file cap).

front: HKLM vs HKCU
back: HKLM = machine (hardware, services). HKCU = current user settings.

front: Deny vs Allow NTFS permissions
back: Explicit Deny wins over Allow.

front: Device Manager scope
back: Hardware only — not applications or services. Launch with devmgmt.msc.

front: Event Viewer: System vs Security logs
back: System = OS/drivers/reboots. Security = logons and permission events.

front: Five main registry hives
back: HKLM, HKCU, HKCR, HKEY_USERS, HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG.

front: MBR vs GPT
back: MBR legacy, 4 primary partitions. GPT modern, UEFI requires GPT.

front: Where is BCD on UEFI?
back: On the ESP (EFI System Partition), not C:\boot.

front: Sleep vs hibernate
back: Sleep keeps RAM powered (fast). Hibernate writes RAM to disk (saves more power).

front: Defrag vs TRIM
back: Defrag HDDs. TRIM SSDs. Do not treat defrag as the SSD fix.

front: Is WinPE a setup pass?
back: No. WinPE is a boot environment. Passes include auditSystem, generalize, auditUser, OOBE.

front: sysprep /generalize does what?
back: Removes hardware-specific drivers and SIDs so the image can run on other PCs.

front: Prepare, capture, deploy tools
back: sysprep prepares. ImageX/DISM captures a .wim. WDS deploys.

front: Correct image workflow order
back: Configure reference PC → sysprep /oobe /generalize /shutdown → WinPE → capture → WDS → PXE → OOBE.

front: Windows 11 Insider on Home?
back: No. Pro, Education, Enterprise only (this guide).

front: Semi-Annual Channel vs LTSC
back: Semi-Annual = regular public releases. LTSC = long-term, few feature changes.

front: bootrec /rebuildbcd vs /fixmbr
back: /rebuildbcd rebuilds BCD (modern/UEFI). /fixmbr repairs the legacy MBR.

front: Windows workstation SMB connection limit
back: 20 concurrent connections.

front: First troubleshooting step
back: Identify the problem — gather symptoms and ask questions before changing the system.

front: Safe Mode with Networking vs minimal
back: Networking adds network drivers so you can download fixes. Minimal is local drivers only.

front: Boot repair order (least to most destructive)
back: Startup Repair → System Restore → bootrec → SFC → Reset this PC → reimage.

front: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL usually means
back: A bad driver. Roll it back in Safe Mode.

front: tracert vs pathping
back: tracert shows the path. pathping shows the path and measures packet loss.

front: Malware removal order
back: Identify/verify → quarantine → remediate → educate.

front: How often should AV definitions update?
back: Daily, not weekly.

front: SFC vs regedit
back: SFC repairs system files. regedit edits the registry. Wrong tool for file corruption.

front: Unactivated Windows restriction
back: Personalization (wallpaper, etc.). Apps and updates still work.

front: DHCP ports
back: UDP 67 server, UDP 68 client.

front: DORA
back: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

front: What is 169.254.x.x?
back: APIPA. DHCP failed. Not a usable routed address.

front: A vs AAAA record
back: A = IPv4. AAAA = IPv6.

front: Can ping IP but not the name
back: DNS problem. Confirm with nslookup.

front: Cannot reach by IP or name
back: Network path / connectivity — not a DNS-only issue.

front: RAID 0 vs RAID 1
back: 0 stripes with no redundancy. 1 mirrors for redundancy.

front: RAID 5 rebuild access (this guide)
back: Cannot access the volume until rebuild finishes.

front: RAID 10 rebuild access (this guide)
back: Can stay online because of mirrored pairs.

front: NAS vs SAN in one line
back: NAS = Ethernet file storage for SMB/home. SAN = high-speed block storage (often Fibre Channel) for enterprise.

front: 3-2-1 backup rule
back: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite. RAID is not a backup.

front: Drill: sysprep command from class
back: sysprep /oobe /generalize /shutdown then capture, then WDS.

front: Memory trick: A vs AAAA
back: One A = IPv4. Four As = IPv6 (bigger).

front: 5 GB file on a USB stick — file system?
back: exFAT or NTFS. FAT32 cannot store files over 4 GB.

front: ipconfig shows 169.254 — next command?
back: ipconfig /release then /renew after checking the DHCP server/cable.

front: Indexing Options vs File Explorer Options
back: Indexing = search catalog. Explorer Options = view/hidden files behavior.

front: Max Ethernet run before attenuation
back: 100 meters (about 328 ft) for any twisted-pair Ethernet.

front: Cat 5e vs Cat 6 vs Cat 6a top speeds
back: 5e = 1 Gb/s (100 m). 6 = 10 Gb/s to 55 m. 6a = 10 Gb/s to 100 m.

front: RJ-45
back: Standard 8P8C connector for Ethernet twisted pair.

front: T568A vs T568B
back: Two 8-wire pinout standards. Both ends must match (straight-through); A on one end + B on other = legacy crossover.

front: Single-mode vs multimode fiber
back: SMF: laser, long haul, 9 micron core. MMF: LED, shorter building runs, 50 or 62.5 micron core.

front: Why fiber beats copper near motors
back: Fiber carries light, so it is immune to EMI and crosstalk.

front: PoE wattages: af / at / bt
Tone generator + probe
back: Traces one cable out of a bundle by sending an audible signal down the wire.

front: Q: Which connectors work with an analog monitor? (choose two)
back: VGA and DVI-A. VGA is the classic analog D-sub; DVI-A is the analog-only DVI variant. HDMI/DisplayPort/DVI-D are digital.

front: Q: USB 2.0 (High Speed) maximum speed?
back: 480 Mbps. (USB 1.1 = 12 Mbps, USB 3.0 = 5 Gbps, USB 3.1 = 10 Gbps, USB4 = 40 Gbps.)

front: Q: What does a YELLOW USB port mean?
back: Always-on charging — it can charge devices even when the PC is powered off. Blue = USB 3.x. Color shows function, not version.

front: Q: Which interface equals DisplayPort + PCIe?
back: Thunderbolt. Thunderbolt 2 = oval mini-DisplayPort connector; Thunderbolt 3/4 = USB-C.

front: Q: Which two standards share the same USB-C connector?
back: Thunderbolt 3 and USB4.

front: Q: eSATA maximum throughput — and does it supply power?
back: 6 Gbps, and NO — eSATA carries data only, no power. It's also slower than USB4/TB3 (40 Gbps).

front: Q: Which power connector for PATA drives and DVD-ROMs?
back: Molex (legacy 4-pin, power only). Modern SATA drives use the SATA power connector.

front: Q: What signal does VGA use?
back: ANALOG. HDMI and DisplayPort are digital; DVI can be analog (DVI-A), digital (DVI-D), or both (DVI-I).

front: Hub (aka repeater) — how does it forward traffic?
back: Repeats every frame received on one port out of ALL other ports. One big collision domain; inefficient and insecure.

front: Switch — why can it send one-to-one (unicast)?
back: It has an ASIC chip with programming that builds a MAC address table (CAM table) mapping MAC+IP to each port; each port is its own collision domain.

front: Router — what does it forward on, and what does it block?
back: Forwards based on IP addresses and routing tables (route print). It does NOT forward broadcasts — every router interface is a broadcast domain boundary.

front: MAC address: length, format, changeable?
back: 48-bit hexadecimal (0-9, A-F), burned into the NIC permanently. Spoofing only changes it in memory. First half = OUI (manufacturer), second half = serial.

front: What does OUI stand for?
back: Organizational Unique Identifier — the first half of a MAC address identifying the manufacturer (e.g., Intel). Exam expects you to know it cold.

front: What is ARP and what does it do?
back: ARP resolves a local IPv4 next hop to a MAC address: the destination host for same-subnet delivery, or the default gateway for a remote destination. Hosts cache ARP mappings (arp -a). Switches separately learn source MAC-to-port mappings from Ethernet frames.

front: What does a broadcast packet look like?
back: Destination IP = all 255s (255.255.255.255); destination MAC = all Fs (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF).

front: TCP vs UDP — one-line each
back: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK), resends unacknowledged packets. UDP: connectionless, no ACKs, used for streaming/VoIP where speed beats reliability.

front: Total port count and the three port ranges
back: 65,536 TCP + 65,536 UDP = 131,072. Well-known 0-1023 (assigned protocols), registered (vendor apps, e.g. SQL 1433), high/dynamic (random client use).

front: QoS vs COS
back: Quality of Service on the LAN; Class of Service on the WAN — and only MPLS supported COS. Both prioritize voice/video traffic.

front: MPLS is legacy — what replaced it?
back: SD-WAN (software-defined WAN, configured on firewall/router, can still do QoS) or site-to-site VPNs over the internet. MPLS's unique feature was Class of Service.

front: Does Ethernet forwarding require every device to know every IP and MAC?
back: No. Switches learn source MAC-to-port mappings from frames. Hosts resolve the IPv4 next hops they need using ARP and cache those mappings. Routing convergence concerns agreement on usable routes; it does not require every host to know every address.

front: Workgroup vs domain — 2 traits each
back: Workgroup (peer-to-peer): not scalable, hard to manage, less secure, profile tied to one PC. Domain (client-server): scalable, manageable, secure, log in anywhere via the domain controller.

front: Network diagram symbols
back: Circle with X (or 4 criss-cross arrows) = router. Rectangle with one arrow = hub. Rectangle with two opposing arrows = switch.

front: PoE — what and why
back: Power over Ethernet: switch delivers low-voltage (<48V) power over the data cable; VoIP phones ship without power bricks. No PoE switch? Use a PoE injector.

front: How does a host choose the ARP target for local versus remote IPv4 delivery?
back: Compare the destination with the local subnet using the mask. Resolve the destination host locally; for a remote destination resolve the on-link default gateway. The packet keeps the remote destination IP.

front: Why did Lab 01’s wrong /24 mask break delivery from PC-A2 to Ops?
back: The approved plan uses /26. With /24, PC-A2 treated remote .74 as local and ARPed on Sales instead of using .1 as its gateway. Compare the mask with the plan and verify the repaired remote path.

front: What should be verified and documented after a next-hop repair?
back: Test relevant local, gateway and previously failed remote reachability. Record configuration, source/destination, tests and results. A successful ping supports tested IP reachability, not proof that every application works.

front: What does a router need to forward a packet?
back: The destination network, matched against its route table. It does not need the host, the origin network, or the return path.

front: Which addresses change at each routed hop, and which stay put (no NAT)?
back: MAC addresses are rebuilt at every hop. Source and destination IPs stay end to end; only TTL and the IPv4 checksum change.

front: Who does a host ARP for when the destination is remote?
back: The default gateway. The destination MAC is the gateway's, but the destination IP is unchanged.

front: How do you view the ARP cache on a host vs a Cisco router?
back: Host (Windows or Mac): arp -a. Cisco router or switch: show ip arp.

front: EtherType values to remember
back: 0x0800 = IPv4, 0x0806 = ARP. The FCS at the end of the frame is a 4-byte CRC that verifies the frame arrived intact.

front: What happens when a router has no matching route and no default route?
back: It drops the packet and sends an ICMP destination unreachable to the sender. The original packet is not returned.

front: Static vs dynamic routing in one line each
back: Static: an admin enters every route by hand and nothing updates itself. Dynamic: protocols share routes and tables update automatically.

front: What is an autonomous system, and which protocols go where?
back: A set of networks under one administrative domain. IGPs (RIP, EIGRP, OSPF) run inside it; the EGP (BGP) runs between autonomous systems.

front: In what order does a router pick among competing routes?
back: 1) Longest matching prefix, 2) lowest administrative distance, 3) lowest metric.

front: Typical administrative distances, lowest to highest
back: Connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120. Lower is more trusted.

front: What are the usable RIP hop counts?
back: 1 to 15. A hop count of 16 or more is unreachable.

front: RIPv2 update method?
back: Multicast to 224.0.0.9 every 30 seconds. It does not broadcast.

front: RIPv1 vs RIPv2: masks and authentication?
back: RIPv1 has neither. RIPv2 sends subnet masks and supports authentication.

front: Order the AD values
back: Connected 0, static 1, EIGRP internal 90, IGRP 100, OSPF 110, RIP 120, external EIGRP 170, unknown 255 (never used).

front: How does AD relate to metrics?
back: Lowest AD wins between sources. Metrics only break ties within the same protocol.

front: How is OSPF cost calculated?
back: Reference bandwidth (100 Mbps) divided by interface bandwidth. Faster links cost less.

front: What is EIGRP's metric?
back: A composite of delay, bandwidth, reliability, and load, weighted by K values.

front: Which protocols are link-state?
back: OSPF and IS-IS. They build the same topology map and run Dijkstra.

front: Does TTL expiry on its own mean there is a routing loop?
back: No. It can also mean the destination is too many hops away. A loop is packets circulating between routers and never arriving.

front: Static vs dynamic routing tradeoff?
back: Static stays until an admin changes it. Dynamic reroutes on failure but costs more RAM, CPU, and bandwidth.

front: What does a switch learn from, source or destination MAC?
back: The source MAC of incoming frames. The destination MAC decides where the frame is forwarded.

front: Unknown destination MAC arrives at a switch. What happens?
back: It floods the frame to all ports in the same VLAN only.

front: Hub vs bridge vs switch
back: Hub: multiport repeater, shared bandwidth. Bridge: software-based, slower. Switch: ASIC hardware, lowest latency.

front: Which VLANs are protected and cannot be deleted?
back: VLAN 1 and VLANs 1002 to 1005. All ports start in VLAN 1.

front: Access port vs trunk port
back: Access: one VLAN, tag removed before the frame leaves. Trunk: many VLANs, tags carried end to end.

front: Where does traffic go on a trunk with no tag?
back: The native VLAN. Tagged traffic is not placed there.

front: 802.1Q tag layout
back: 4 bytes between source MAC and type field: 16-bit TPID 0x8100, 3-bit CoS, 1-bit DEI, 12-bit VLAN ID.

front: STP root bridge and timing
back: Lowest priority wins (lowest MAC on a tie). Default port state is blocking; 50 seconds to forwarding.

front: Steps to segment R&D with flexibility
back: New VLAN, routed SVI, ACLs on the VLAN interface. Extended ACLs cannot go on layer 2 ports.

front: CoS vs ToS/DiffServ, PoE, VTP
back: CoS: layer 2, 3 bits in the tag, 8 queues. ToS/DiffServ: layer 3. 802.3at: 25.5 W. VTP propagates the VLAN database.

front: What do NDP and router advertisements do in IPv6?
back: NDP discovers neighboring devices. Router advertisements (RA) announce the gateway so hosts can find it.

front: Dual stack vs tunneling?
back: Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side. Tunneling carries IPv6 inside IPv4 (Teredo, ISATAP).

front: Internal vs external EIGRP AD?
back: Internal EIGRP 90. External EIGRP (routes redistributed into EIGRP) 170.

front: What does an AD of 255 mean?
back: The route source is unknown. The router never uses a route with AD 255.

front: Two updates list the same remote network. What does the router check first?
back: Administrative distance. The route with the lower AD is placed in the routing table.

front: What is the Class A first-octet range and default split?
back: 1 through 126, 8 network bits and 24 host bits.

front: What is the Class B first-octet range and default split?
back: 128 through 191, 16 network bits and 16 host bits.

front: What is the Class C first-octet range and default split?
back: 192 through 223, 24 network bits and 8 host bits.

front: What are the three RFC 1918 private ranges?
What does an address in 169.254.0.1 to 169.254.255.254 tell you?
back: APIPA: the client could not reach DHCP and configured itself, with mask 255.255.0.0.

front: Which class are Class D and Class E addresses?
back: D (224 to 239) is multicast. E (240 to 255) is experimental.

front: How long is an IPv6 address and how is it written?
back: 128 bits, written in hexadecimal. IPv4 is 32 bits in decimal.

front: Link-local vs unique local IPv6 addresses?
back: Both are non-Internet. Link-local is never routed. Unique local can be routed inside the organization.

front: Name three IPv6 compatibility methods.
back: Tunneling (IPv6 inside IPv4), dual stack (both side by side), and NAT64 (translate between IPv6 and IPv4).

front: How does EUI-64 build an IPv6 interface ID from a MAC address?
back: Insert FF:FE in the middle of the 48-bit MAC and invert the 7th bit of the first byte.

front: What defines a unicast address?
back: An address assigned to a single interface: one-to-one communication.

front: What defines a multicast address?
back: A one-to-many address, delivered to multiple interfaces.

front: What is an anycast address?
back: One address on multiple interfaces where the packet is delivered only to the first (nearest) one found: one-to-nearest.

front: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
back: ::1, the IPv6 version of 127.0.0.1.

front: What does an IPv6 link-local address always start with?
back: FE80::/10. It is not meant to be routed.

front: What does an IPv6 unique local address start with, and what is it like?
back: FC00::/7. Not routed to the Internet but still globally unique. Formerly called site-local.

front: Which IPv6 type is used like a regular public routable IPv4 address?
back: Global unicast.

front: What is the name for the 48-bit (6-byte) address physically assigned to a NIC?
back: A MAC address, also called a hardware address or burned-in address.

front: How many more bits does IPv6 have than IPv4?
back: 96 more: 128 bits compared with 32 bits.

front: What range counts as loopback in IPv4?
back: 127.0.0.1 through 127.255.255.254, used for loopback and diagnostics.

front: What are the default subnet masks for Class A, B, and C?
What are the big five subnetting questions?
back: How many subnets? How many hosts per subnet? What are the valid subnets? What is the broadcast address of each? What are the valid hosts?

front: How do you find the number of subnets?
back: 2 to the power of the subnet bits. One bit on in the interesting octet gives 2^1 = 2 subnets.

front: How do you find the hosts per subnet?
back: 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. A /25 has 7 host bits: 2^7 - 2 = 126.

front: Why do you subtract 2 from the host count?
back: One address is the subnet address (all host bits off) and one is the broadcast (all host bits on). Neither can be given to a host.

front: How do you find the block size?
back: 256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet. For 255.255.255.128: 256 - 128 = 128.

front: How do you find a subnet's broadcast address?
back: Take the number right before the next subnet. All host bits are on. For the 0 subnet in a /25, that is 127.

front: What are the valid hosts in a subnet?
back: Everything between the subnet address and the broadcast address.
2 subnets (0 and 128), 126 hosts each, broadcasts 127 and 255, hosts 1 to 126 and 129 to 254.

front: Class C /26 (255.255.255.192): block size, subnets, hosts?
back: Block size 64, 4 subnets, 62 hosts per subnet.

front: Class C /27 (255.255.255.224): block size, subnets, hosts?
back: Block size 32, 8 subnets, 30 hosts per subnet.

front: Which mask is best for a point-to-point WAN link, and why?
back: 255.255.255.252 (/30). It has 2 usable hosts, exactly the two ends of the link, and wastes nothing.

front: How many addresses does a /24 waste on a two-address WAN link?
back: 252 (254 hosts minus the 2 used).

front: What does CIDR notation tell you?
back: How many bits of the mask are on, written after a slash. 255.255.255.0 is /24.

front: What is a classful network versus classless routing?
back: Classful uses the same mask on every host and router interface. Classless lets different size masks be used (VLSM).

front: What is the difference between static NAT, dynamic NAT, and PAT?
back: Static: fixed one-to-one mapping. Dynamic: public addresses taken from a pool. PAT (NAT overloading): many hosts share one public address, separated by port numbers.

front: Which two names mean the same NAT feature?
back: NAT overloading and port address translation (PAT).

front: What is the network ID and host ID of 192.168.10.77 with mask 255.255.255.0?
back: Network ID 192.168.10 (the first three octets). Host ID 77 (the last octet).

front: Where does BGP sit in the routing tree?
back: In the EGP branch. It runs between autonomous systems and is path-vector. It is not an IGP and not hybrid.

front: Which branch of the IGP splits into distance vector and link state?
back: Dynamic routing splits into IGP (inside one AS) and EGP (between ASs). IGP splits again into distance vector (RIP, IGRP) and link state (OSPF, IS-IS). EIGRP is hybrid.

front: What is split horizon?
back: A loop-prevention rule. A router does not advertise a route back out the interface it learned that route on.

front: Which distance-vector protocols use split horizon?
back: RIP and IGRP. Split horizon prevents a route from being sent back to the router that advertised it.

front: What does nonrepudiation provide?
back: Proof that a sender cannot later deny having sent a message, often through a digital signature.

front: Authentication versus authorization?
back: Authentication verifies identity. Authorization decides what that identity may do.

front: Which encryption protects Wi-Fi traffic at Layer 2?
back: WPA2 and WPA3. MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) protects Ethernet frames on a single link.

front: What UDP ports does RADIUS use?
back: UDP 1812 for authentication and UDP 1813 for accounting (RFC 2865 and RFC 2866).

front: How does RADIUS encryption differ from TACACS+?
back: RADIUS encrypts only the password. TACACS+ encrypts the full payload and uses TCP 49.

front: Which UDP ports carry SNMP polls and traps?
back: Polls use UDP 161. Traps use UDP 162.

front: What does a hash provide, and does it use a key?
back: Integrity: a one-way, fixed-length digest. It uses no key and does not provide confidentiality.

front: What does the CIA triad stand for?
back: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

front: What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?
back: A vulnerability is a weakness. An exploit is code or a technique that takes advantage of it.

front: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
back: A weakness the vendor has no patch or workaround for yet.

front: What does EDR do differently from traditional antivirus?
back: It analyzes behavior and patterns, often with machine learning, so it can catch zero-day activity that signatures miss.

front: What does a CRL contain, and who publishes it?
back: A list of revoked certificates, published by the certificate authority.

front: What is the AIA extension used for?
back: It tells the client where to fetch the issuing CA's certificate.

front: Which regulation protects EU consumer personal data?
back: GDPR, the General Data Protection Regulation.

front: Layer 4 of the OSI model?
back: Transport. Its PDU is the segment; TCP and UDP live here.

front: OSI layers 1 to 7 mnemonic?
back: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

front: OSI layers 7 to 1 mnemonic?
back: All People Seem To Need Data Processing: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

front: PDU at layers 4, 3, 2, and 1?
back: Segment, packet, frame, bits.

front: DoD Process/Application layer maps to which OSI layers?
back: Application, Presentation, and Session (7, 6, 5).

front: DoD Host-to-Host layer maps to?
back: OSI Transport (layer 4).

front: DoD Internet layer maps to?
back: OSI Network (layer 3).

front: DoD Network Access layer maps to?
back: OSI Data Link and Physical (layers 2 and 1).

front: MDI versus MDI-X devices?
back: MDI: PCs, servers, routers. MDI-X: switches and hubs.

front: When do you use a straight-through cable?
back: Between unlike devices (MDI to MDI-X), such as PC to switch, PC to hub, router to switch, router to hub.

front: When do you use a crossover cable?
back: Between like devices: switch to switch, switch to hub, hub to hub, PC to PC, router to router, PC to router.

front: Router to hub: straight-through or crossover?
back: Straight-through. The layer shortcut (odd to odd) says crossover, but router and hub are MDI to MDI-X.

front: What does Auto-MDIX do?
back: Detects the pairs and swaps transmit and receive inside the port, so either cable type works.

front: Which pins does a 10/100 crossover swap?
back: Pins 1 and 2 swap with 3 and 6 (T568A on one end, T568B on the other).

front: Which two components must support virtualization?
back: The CPU (Intel VT-x or AMD-V) and the BIOS/UEFI.

front: PC loses its date and time after power loss. Fix?
back: Replace the CMOS battery (and repair the UPS if it was supposed to keep power on).

front: What attaches a heat sink to a CPU?
back: Thermal paste.

front: Forgotten BIOS password: which motherboard part resets it?
back: The CMOS clear (password reset) jumper.

front: Fastest desktop storage technology?
back: NVMe (SSD over PCIe lanes).

front: Server must stay up if a PSU fails. Which PSU?
back: A redundant power supply.

front: Integrated video failed and you add a PCIe card. Two true statements?
back: It is usually detected automatically, and you might need to disable integrated video in BIOS.

front: Which connectors carry power and data?
back: Lightning, USB-C, and micro-USB. Molex is power only; DB-9 is data only.

front: EP process steps in order?
back: Processing, charging, exposing, developing, transferring, fusing, cleaning (People Can't Ever Do The Funky Chicken).

front: Which EP step uses the laser?
back: Exposing. Developing adds toner; transferring moves it to paper.

front: Printer for multipart (triplicate) forms?
back: Impact (dot-matrix).

front: Type 1 vs Type 2 hypervisor?
back: Type 1 runs on bare metal (fastest). Type 2 runs on a host OS.

front: Coax connector types?
back: F-type (cable TV/modem) and BNC. SC is fiber; RJ-45 is twisted pair.

front: Multimode vs single-mode fiber distance?
back: Multimode: short runs, a few hundred meters up to about 2 km. Single-mode: tens of kilometers.

front: Bridges, hubs, routers: which OSI layers?
back: Bridge: Data Link (2). Hub: Physical (1). Router: Network (3).

front: APIPA range and mask?
A record vs PTR record?
back: A: name to IPv4 address. PTR: IP address to name.

front: TCP three-way handshake?
back: SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK.

front: What can command-and-control traffic establish about an incident?
back: It can indicate commands to compromised systems. C2 supports DDoS and other malware activity; identify the actual behavior before classifying the attack.

front: Evil twin vs rogue AP?
back: An evil twin impersonates a legitimate wireless network. A rogue AP is unauthorized; it need not impersonate an SSID or be attached to the organization’s wired LAN.

front: Layer 2 switch forwards by?
back: Destination MAC address, looked up in the MAC address (CAM) table.

front: Router forwards by?
back: Destination IP address, looked up in the routing table.

front: Layer 3 (multilayer) switch?
back: A switch with a hardware routing engine: switches by MAC inside a VLAN and routes by IP between VLANs.

front: SVI?
back: Switch virtual interface: a virtual Layer 3 interface for a VLAN. Its IP is the default gateway for hosts in that VLAN.

front: What changes when a packet is routed?
back: Both MAC addresses are rewritten and TTL drops by 1. Source and destination IP stay the same (unless NAT).

front: What changes when a frame is switched at Layer 2?
back: Nothing in the addresses: MACs, IPs, and TTL are unchanged.

front: Cisco command to enable routing on a Layer 3 switch?
back: ip routing

front: Router-on-a-stick?
back: One router interface on an 802.1Q trunk with a subinterface per VLAN, used for inter-VLAN routing.

front: Layer 3 switch vs router at the edge?
back: Layer 3 switch: fast inter-VLAN routing, many Ethernet ports. Router: NAT, VPN, WAN links, internet edge.

front: Broadcast domains on a Layer 2 switch?
back: One per VLAN. Collision domains: one per port.

front: Unknown unicast on a Layer 2 switch?
back: Flooded out every port in the same VLAN except the one it arrived on.

front: no switchport?
back: Makes a Layer 3 switch port a routed port that takes an IP address like a router interface.

front: Three-way handshake?
back: SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK.

front: TCP graceful close?
back: FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK (four segments). RST aborts immediately.

front: IPv4 protocol numbers to know?
back: 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 47 GRE, 50 ESP, 51 AH.

front: Port ranges?
back: Well-known 0-1023, registered 1024-49151, dynamic (ephemeral) 49152-65535.

front: TCP vs UDP in one line?
back: TCP: connection-oriented, acknowledged, ordered, windowed. UDP: connectionless, no ACKs, low overhead.

front: Socket?
back: IP address plus port, for example 192.168.1.20:51544.

front: SNMP ports?
back: UDP 161 for polling and UDP 162 for traps.

front: Secure versions and ports?
back: SSH 22 (not Telnet 23), HTTPS 443 (not HTTP 80), LDAPS 636 (not LDAP 389), SIP TLS 5061 (not 5060).

front: DNS transport?
back: UDP 53 for queries; TCP 53 for zone transfers and large replies.

front: SMB, RDP, SQL Server ports?
back: SMB 445, RDP 3389, SQL Server 1433.

front: TTL?
back: Decremented by 1 per router hop; at 0 the packet is dropped and ICMP Time Exceeded is sent.

front: ESP vs AH?
back: ESP encrypts and authenticates; AH authenticates only (no encryption).

front: HTML?
back: HyperText Markup Language: describes page structure with elements. Markup, not a programming language.

front: URL to page steps?
back: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS (HTTPS), HTTP GET, response with status + HTML, render and fetch CSS/JS/images.

front: HTTP status classes?
back: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
404: page not found (path missing). 500: server application failed. Either way the network worked.

front: HTTP vs HTTPS ports?
back: HTTP TCP 80; HTTPS TCP 443.

front: HTML vs CSS vs JavaScript?
back: HTML structure, CSS presentation, JavaScript behavior.

front: GET vs POST?
back: GET retrieves a resource; POST sends data (forms) to the server.

front: 502 Bad Gateway?
back: A proxy or load balancer got an invalid response from the server behind it.

front: See raw HTML or headers?
back: View Source (Ctrl+U) for HTML; curl -I or dev tools Network tab for status and headers.

front: Connection refused vs timed out?
back: Refused: host reached, nothing listening on the port. Timed out: no reply (path, firewall, or host down).

front: What should you compare before replacing hardware for a “no signal” message?
back: Compare the physical input socket with the selected input, then confirm the computer is sending an external image. A working display menu does not prove the cable or input path works.

front: How can a known-good cable help isolate a flashing display?
back: Keep the source, ports, mode, and display unchanged. If replacing only the cable removes the symptom, the original cable path is implicated; flashing alone does not prove panel failure.

front: Why can a passive DVI-A-to-DVI-D cable fail even if its ends fit?
back: DVI-A is analog and DVI-D is digital. A passive cable does not translate signals. Use supported active conversion in the source-to-display direction, checking modes, connectors, and power.

front: How do you distinguish fuzzy projector text from geometric distortion?
back: Compare the projector menu/test pattern and source image. Check focus, placement, and native resolution for blur; check placement, aspect ratio, and documented keystone controls for sizing or shape distortion.

front: Does a faint old logo prove permanent burn-in?
back: No. Temporary image retention may fade; lasting wear is burn-in. Identify the panel/model, follow supported maintenance guidance, and escalate persistent marks without promising a software cure.

front: What is a safe response to persistent dark or bright pixel dots?
back: Use the manufacturer’s test, record positions/counts, and consult that model’s support policy. Do not press the panel or promise that pixel-fixing software repairs dead pixels.

front: What should you check before treating a dim or shutting-down projector as a failed lamp?
back: Identify lamp versus laser/LED technology; check settings, input, diagnostic indicators, ventilation and sleep timing using the model guide. Confirm the fault before authorized lamp service; follow its cooling and disconnection procedure.

front: HDMI video works, but there is no sound. What comes first?
back: Confirm speakers exist and check the selected audio output, mute and volume. HDMI can carry audio, but working video does not prove audio is routed to that display.

front: Confirmed burnt-out projector bulb: safe repair sequence?
back: Follow the model manual: shut down, disconnect power before opening, allow specified cooling, replace approved lamp module, then reset usage timer and verify operation.

front: Incorrect colors: how do you separate cable/settings from panel faults?
back: Compare the internal test, reset unintended color settings, and try a known-good cable. A defect in the internal test points toward the display.

front: Sizing issues: which controls match which symptoms?
back: Small projected frame: distance/zoom. Cropped edges: overscan/fit. Stretched picture: aspect ratio. Only UI/text too small: desktop scaling.

front: What proves a display repair is complete?
back: Retest the intended source, mode, image/audio, and original workload. For shutdown faults, run past the prior failure interval; document cause, fix, and prevention.

front: DoS vs DDoS: what does distributed describe?
back: Multiple attack sources. It does not specify reflection or amplification.

front: Reflection vs amplification?
back: Reflection sends third-party replies toward a spoofed victim source. Amplification increases response traffic relative to the attacker’s request. Both can occur together.

front: Does C2 traffic prove DDoS?
back: No. C2 directs compromised systems and supports several malicious activities; seek evidence of the actual task.

front: What does MAC flooding pressure?
back: The switch’s MAC learning/forwarding table. Unknown destinations may be flooded within the VLAN; behavior varies by platform.

front: Name two VLAN-hopping mechanisms.
back: Unwanted trunk negotiation (switch spoofing) and double tagging under susceptible native-VLAN conditions.

front: ARP poisoning vs MAC spoofing?
back: ARP poisoning installs false IP-to-MAC bindings using forged address-resolution information. MAC spoofing changes the address an interface presents.

front: DNS spoofing vs cache poisoning?
back: Spoofing supplies a forged answer; cache poisoning stores false data for later use. The terms can overlap.

front: Does DNSSEC encrypt queries?
back: No. Validation provides origin authentication and integrity for signed DNS data with an appropriate trust chain.

front: Which DHCP options can redirect a client?
back: Router/default-gateway and DNS-server options. Compare them with approved configuration and identify the offering server.

front: Rogue AP vs evil twin?
back: A rogue AP is unauthorized. An evil twin impersonates a legitimate wireless network. It need not be wired into the victim LAN or use a specific channel.

front: Does a duplicate SSID prove an evil twin?
back: No. Legitimate APs share SSIDs; compare inventory, authentication settings, and other evidence.

front: What distinguishes an on-path attacker?
back: A position between parties that enables relaying, observation, or manipulation. Credential theft alone does not establish that position.

front: Name the evidence source each social method abuses.
back: Phishing: deceptive communication. Dumpster diving: discarded information. Shoulder surfing: observed entry or display. Tailgating: another person’s physical access.

front: Can antimalware guarantee protection from phishing?
back: No. Credential phishing may involve no malware. Use layered messaging, identity, endpoint, and user-verification controls.

front: 802.1X vs NAC posture?
back: 802.1X controls authenticated admission. Posture checks evaluate endpoint compliance; authentication alone does not prove up-to-date protection.

front: Why is MAC filtering weaker than device authentication?
back: A presented MAC address can be copied; it is not a cryptographic proof of identity.

front: What does an ACL direction mean?
back: Inbound or outbound relative to the interface where it is applied. Platform limits must be stated with the platform.

front: What makes segmentation enforce access policy?
back: An enforced boundary such as ACLs/firewalls with allowed and denied flows. VLAN creation alone does not restrict routed traffic.

front: Honeypot vs honeynet?
back: One monitored decoy versus a network of decoys. Isolate and monitor them; they are detection aids, not replacements for prevention.

front: Why treat OT security changes differently?
back: Physical-process safety, availability, and device support constrain changes. Coordinate with process owners and test through an approved plan.

front: What is the first source for an unfamiliar laptop replacement?
back: The manufacturer’s service guide/parts list for the exact model and configuration; verify connector, part number, safety steps and required post-repair tests.

front: Does a battery-health percentage alone require replacement?
back: No. Compare vendor diagnostics, reported behavior, age and model guidance; replacement thresholds are product-specific.

front: When should you “calibrate” a lithium-ion battery gauge?
back: Only when the applicable device/vendor procedure calls for that model and symptom. A gauge recalibration cannot restore worn chemical capacity; do not make routine full discharges a general rule.

front: What should you do if a lithium-ion battery is swollen or leaking?
back: Stop use/charging when safe, do not press, bend, puncture or remove it, and follow the manufacturer’s safety/service guidance.

front: Why is charger wattage not enough to prove compatibility?
back: The device must also support the connector, voltage/current or USB-PD profile, cable capability, power direction, model requirements and (for some barrel adapters) identification method.

front: Which display uses the classic laptop “inverter” description?
back: A CCFL-backlit LCD, where an inverter drives the fluorescent backlight. LED-backlit LCDs use LED-driver circuitry; OLED has no separate backlight.

front: What does Mini-LED describe?
back: An LCD display with a dense LED backlight, often local dimming; the LCD layer still forms the image.

front: Can DDR4 SO-DIMM replace a DDR3 SO-DIMM because both are laptop RAM?
back: No. DDR generations use different electrical/keying requirements. Check the exact model support, module type, capacity and speed.

front: What can cause weak Wi-Fi after a laptop display repair?
back: A displaced, damaged, pinched or incorrectly routed Wi-Fi antenna lead is one possibility; check model routing and verify before replacing the radio card.

front: Before replacing a camera or microphone, what reversible checks help?
back: Check the hardware shutter/mute switch, OS privacy permission, selected device, application setting and built-in diagnostics.

front: Does a USB-C connector guarantee charging, video, or a particular data speed?
back: No. USB-C is a connector shape. The port, cable and endpoints must support the needed data/video/power feature and negotiated mode.

front: Can Bluetooth tethering share a phone’s internet connection?
back: Yes, when the phone, client OS/profile, carrier and settings support it. Pair and test the connection; Wi-Fi and USB tethering are other supported options on some devices.

front: What is NFC useful for when connecting accessories?
back: A very short-range tap can exchange a small record, tag data, or Bluetooth-pairing information. NFC is not a generic sustained high-throughput accessory link.

front: How does a port replicator differ from a docking station?
back: A port replicator repeats supported ports; a dock may add other controllers, displays or power. The product/model’s actual host and feature compatibility decides.

front: Does a webcam that fails in one meeting app prove camera hardware failure?
back: No. Check shutter, OS permission, selected input, app permission/settings and diagnostics before suspecting a part.

front: What is a digitizer?
back: The sensing layer/system that converts pen or touch input into coordinates; it may be bonded into the display assembly rather than serviceable separately.

front: Which IEEE family underlies Wi-Fi 6?
back: 802.11ax; supported band depends on the AP/client.

front: What does Wi-Fi 6E add to Wi-Fi 6?
back: Use of 6 GHz by compatible 802.11ax devices where local rules permit it.

front: Which bands can 802.11n use?
back: 2.4 GHz and/or 5 GHz, depending on the device.

front: Does 802.11ac operate at 6 GHz?
back: No; 802.11ac/Wi-Fi 5 is a 5 GHz generation. 6 GHz Wi-Fi 6E is based on 802.11ax.

front: Why is 2.4 GHz often a range choice, not a guaranteed speed choice?
back: It may propagate farther indoors, but has fewer practical channels and often more interference. Real performance depends on the environment and devices.

front: What changes as channel width grows?
back: The channel occupies more spectrum and may raise a compatible link’s PHY rate, but there may be fewer usable choices and more overlap/congestion.

front: Are channels 1, 6 and 11 a universal Wi-Fi plan?
back: No. They are a common 20 MHz U.S. 2.4 GHz plan. Country rules, device support, width and local interference matter.

front: What is DFS for?
back: Radar sharing on selected bands/channels: compatible APs detect radar and change or stop use as regulation requires.

front: What does beamforming do?
back: It can improve signal quality toward a client and may improve performance; it does not guarantee range or throughput.

front: What does OFDMA add in Wi-Fi 6/7?
back: Resource-unit scheduling lets compatible clients share a channel more efficiently for some traffic patterns; it does not guarantee each client’s peak rate.

front: What does BSS coloring identify?
back: A compatible device can distinguish its own BSS from an overlapping BSS; spatial reuse may be possible for sufficiently weak neighboring signals. It does not erase interference.

front: What is MLO in Wi-Fi 7?
back: A supported multi-link operation in which compatible AP and client devices can use multiple links under the selected configuration.

front: Why is a Wi-Fi PHY rate different from an internet speed test?
back: PHY rate is a link signaling rate; overhead, contention, retries, signal, client/AP capability, backhaul and ISP plan reduce actual application throughput.

front: What does WPA3-Personal use for authentication/key establishment?
back: SAE. Cipher selection/data protection is a separate part of the negotiated security suite.

front: Does “AES” uniquely tell you the Wi-Fi generation?
back: No. WPA2 and WPA3 modes can use AES-family ciphers. Identify authentication/key-management and cipher settings separately.

front: What can MAC filtering prove about the device that joined?
back: Only that the presented address matched a configured list; MAC addresses can be copied, so filtering is not strong device authentication.

front: Does hiding or changing the SSID encrypt Wi-Fi traffic?
back: No. Use an appropriate authenticated/encrypted security mode; SSID choice is a network name.

front: What does a 169.254.x.x IPv4 address suggest on a DHCP client?
back: Automatic configuration did not obtain a usable lease. Check association, link, DHCP server/scope and path; the address alone does not identify the exact cause.
